newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli think tank chief sounds war warning.
newsitem.headline: Israeli think tank chief sounds war warning.

text.p: The head of a leading Israeli strategic studies centre said on Tuesday a continued freeze in peace talks with Syria would raise significantly the chances of war between the two countries.

Zeev Maoz, head of Tel Aviv University's Jaffee Centre for Strategic Studies, said on the release of its 1994-1995 Middle East Military Balance report that Israel maintained a qualitative edge over Syria but should increase its preparedness for war.
"In my assessment, as long as the political stalemate continues, the probability of war rises in a very significant way," he said.
"We need of course to deal with current problems such as ensuring we have sufficient military stockpiles for the long term," Maoz told Israel Radio.
Israeli-Syrian negotiations, begun in 1991 and held only intermittently, are frozen over the future of the Golan Heights, captured by Israel in the 1967 Middle East war.
Policy guidelines of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party say Israel must maintain sovereignty over the strategic plateau.
Syrian troop movements from Lebanon to positions within striking distance of Israeli positions on the Golan last September caused war jitters in the Jewish state.
Maoz said that even if war did not break out in 1997, Israel must take into account that Syria would apparently respond to a further peace stalemate by "resuming the arms race between them and us".

Syria began an effort to achieve "strategic parity" with Israel in the 1970s but the dismantling of the Soviet Union, its main weapons supplier, and a faltering economy slowed the modernisation of its military.
Nonetheless, Maoz called Syria's Scud missile arsenal a "real threat" and the only area in which the strategic balance with Israel had been altered.
"It is the main area in which Syria has invested in acquisition and self-development," he said, referring to the purchase of Scud missiles and production ability from North Korea.
"We definitely should take into account that in any war scenario, these weapons will be used," Maoz added.
The centre's report said Syria had a "substantial pile" of locally developed chemical warheads for its Scuds, which the survey numbered at 26.

Last September, South Korea's unification ministry said North Korea had exported about 400 Scud B and C missiles to the Middle East and sold plants and machinery equipment for their manufacture to Syria and Iran.
